sql_runner.py:95 reads cap = effective_row_cap(self._max_rows) in the caller's task, then passes it to asyncio.to_thread (line 96) and _run_sql_blocking uses it at 134-135. effective_row_cap (limits.py:51-54) only reads get_effective_settings(), which reads the ContextVar _PROFILE_VAR (runtime.py:54,71) and returns min(constructor, effective.max_rows) or the constructor cap. It is a pure read with no side effects, so reading it once before dispatch yields the same value as the old in-line call. For write-shaped SQL the cap is now read but unused (line 137-139), which is harmless because the read has no side effects. The claim's wording is hedged ('does propagate/not propagate'); to_thread copies the context anyway, and the pre-read is equivalent either way.

sql_runner.py:91-93 says a configured statement timeout bounds the orphaned worker thread. Defaults: MySQLRunner.__init__ statement_timeout_ms=0 (line 30, disabled); config.py:58-59 defaults to 30000. But the file's own note at lines 120-123 says MAX_EXECUTION_TIME is a no-op for non-SELECTs. With read_only=False (a supported setting), a long UPDATE/DELETE goes through the DictCursor path (lines 143-146) and is not bounded by the timeout, so the thread outlives a cancelled caller. The comment is unqualified and so is wrong for that path. It is only a comment, so the impact is small.
